argument: Steve lays out Marx's critique of capitalism, arguing that every economic system, including capitalism, has 'internal conflicts' built into its structure that make it eventually unsustainable, the same forces that ended feudalism and slavery. Capitalism's version is that cutting wages to raise capital shrinks the buying power of the very workers who are also its consumers, so it cannibalizes itself over time; meanwhile the specialization that lets capitalism mass-produce goods (started with the Enclosure Acts displacing people into factories) alienates workers from a sense of purpose and leaves them fearing their own expendability. Marx's deeper claim is that profit itself is a euphemism for theft, the gap between what a worker produces and what they're paid, and that even capitalism's crashes are not natural but a hallmark of a system that outproduces what people can actually buy, so he'd argue that whatever problems communism has are more manageable than the severe ones capitalism already causes.
keyIdeas: Marx calls 'internal conflicts' the competing forces built into the structure of an economic system itself, the same kind that made feudalism and slavery eventually unsustainable and led to revolution.

Capitalism 'cannibalizes itself' because cutting wages to increase capital also cuts the buying power of the workers who are also the consumers of what's produced, so the rich keep getting richer while demand shrinks.

The Enclosure Acts converted common land into private property, displacing people who then had little choice but to move into factories and mills, feeding the specialization and division of labor that let capitalism mass-produce goods efficiently.

Specialization massively increases output (the clockmaker example) but alienates workers from a sense of purpose, since doing one small, repetitive task all day (like capping sriracha bottles) makes it hard to see yourself in your work.

Marx calls profit a euphemism for theft: the gap between what a worker actually produces in value and what they're paid is pocketed by those who control production rather than reflecting what the worker is actually worth.
